questions.question_es: ¿Cuál de los siguientes es un nombre de variable válido en Python?
questions.question_en: Which of the following is a valid variable name in Python?
questions.explanation_es: Un identificador no puede empezar con un dígito ('2var'), no puede contener guiones ('my-var', el guion se interpreta como resta) y no puede ser una palabra reservada ('class'). '_my_var' es válido: puede empezar con guion bajo y contener letras, números y guiones bajos.
questions.explanation_en: An identifier cannot start with a digit ('2var'), cannot contain hyphens ('my-var', the hyphen is parsed as subtraction), and cannot be a reserved keyword ('class'). '_my_var' is valid: it can start with an underscore and contain letters, digits, and underscores.
questions.source: CPython docs 3.13 — The Python Language Reference: Execution model (naming and binding) — https://docs.python.org/3/reference/executionmodel.html#naming-and-binding

questions.question_es: En Python debes declarar el tipo de una variable antes de asignarle un valor.
questions.question_en: In Python you must declare a variable's type before assigning it a value.
questions.explanation_es: Python es de tipado dinámico: el tipo se infiere en tiempo de ejecución a partir del valor asignado. Simplemente escribes `x = 5` y Python determina que `x` es un `int`, sin necesidad de declarar `int x` como en lenguajes de tipado estático.
questions.explanation_en: Python is dynamically typed: the type is inferred at runtime from the assigned value. You simply write `x = 5` and Python determines that `x` is an `int`, with no need to declare `int x` as in statically typed languages.
questions.source: CPython docs 3.13 — The Python Language Reference: Execution model (naming and binding) — https://docs.python.org/3/reference/executionmodel.html#naming-and-binding

questions.question_es:
¿Qué imprime el siguiente código?
```python
x = 5
y = x
x = 10
print(y)
```
questions.question_en:
What does the following code print?
```python
x = 5
y = x
x = 10
print(y)
```
questions.explanation_es: `y = x` hace que `y` apunte al mismo objeto entero `5` al que apunta `x` en ese momento. Como los enteros son inmutables, reasignar `x = 10` simplemente hace que `x` apunte a un objeto distinto (`10`); `y` sigue enlazada al `5` original.
questions.explanation_en: `y = x` makes `y` point to the same integer object `5` that `x` points to at that moment. Since integers are immutable, reassigning `x = 10` just makes `x` point to a different object (`10`); `y` remains bound to the original `5`.
questions.source: CPython docs 3.13 — The Python Language Reference: Execution model (naming and binding) — https://docs.python.org/3/reference/executionmodel.html#naming-and-binding

questions.question_es:
¿Qué imprime el siguiente código?
```python
a, b = 1, 2
a, b = b, a
print(a, b)
```
questions.question_en:
What does the following code print?
```python
a, b = 1, 2
a, b = b, a
print(a, b)
```
questions.explanation_es: `a, b = b, a` es el idioma clásico de Python para intercambiar valores. El lado derecho se evalúa por completo primero, construyendo la tupla `(2, 1)` con los valores originales, y luego se desempaqueta en `a` y `b`, dejando `a=2, b=1`.
questions.explanation_en: `a, b = b, a` is the classic Python idiom for swapping values. The right-hand side is fully evaluated first, building the tuple `(2, 1)` from the original values, then it is unpacked into `a` and `b`, leaving `a=2, b=1`.
questions.source: CPython docs 3.13 — The Python Language Reference: Execution model (naming and binding) — https://docs.python.org/3/reference/executionmodel.html#naming-and-binding

questions.question_es: Completa el código para comprobar si `x` no está enlazada a ningún valor: `if x ___ None:`
questions.question_en: Complete the code to check whether `x` is bound to no value: `if x ___ None:`
questions.explanation_es: Se recomienda usar el operador `is` (identidad) en lugar de `==` para comparar con `None`, porque `None` es un singleton único en memoria y `is` evita depender de un posible `__eq__` sobrecargado en la clase de `x`.
questions.explanation_en: It is recommended to use the `is` operator (identity) instead of `==` when comparing with `None`, because `None` is a unique singleton in memory and `is` avoids relying on a possibly overridden `__eq__` on `x`'s class.
questions.source: PEP 8 — Programming Recommendations (comparisons to None use 'is'/'is not') — https://peps.python.org/pep-0008/

questions.question_es: ¿Cuál de las siguientes afirmaciones sobre la asignación de variables en Python es VERDADERA?
questions.question_en: Which of the following statements about variable assignment in Python is TRUE?
options_es: Las variables son contenedores que almacenan el valor directamente
Las variables deben ser inmutables una vez asignadas
Las variables son nombres enlazados a objetos; la asignación enlaza un nombre a un objeto sin copiarlo
Asignar un nuevo valor a una variable modifica el objeto original en su lugar
options_en: Variables are containers that store the value directly
Variables must be immutable once assigned
Variables are names bound to objects; assignment binds a name to an object without copying it
Assigning a new value to a variable modifies the original object in place
questions.explanation_es: Python usa un modelo de 'nombres y objetos': una variable es solo una referencia (etiqueta) hacia un objeto en memoria. `x = valor` crea o reutiliza un objeto y enlaza el nombre `x` a él; no hay copia implícita ni una 'caja' fija que contenga el valor, a diferencia de lenguajes con variables de tipo valor.
questions.explanation_en: Python uses a 'names and objects' model: a variable is just a reference (label) pointing to an object in memory. `x = value` creates or reuses an object and binds the name `x` to it; there is no implicit copy or fixed 'box' holding the value, unlike languages with value-type variables.
questions.source: CPython docs 3.13 — The Python Language Reference: Data model (objects, values, and names)

questions.question_es: ¿Cuál es el tipo del valor `3.14` en Python?
questions.question_en: What is the type of the value `3.14` in Python?
questions.explanation_es: Cualquier número escrito con punto decimal es del tipo `float` en Python, incluso si su parte decimal es cero (por ejemplo `3.0` también es `float`).
questions.explanation_en: Any number written with a decimal point is of type `float` in Python, even if its decimal part is zero (for example `3.0` is also a `float`).
questions.source: CPython docs 3.13 — Built-in Types: Numeric Types (int, float, complex)

questions.question_es: En Python 3, el operador `/` siempre devuelve un `float`, incluso al dividir dos enteros de forma exacta (por ejemplo `10 / 2`).
questions.question_en: In Python 3, the `/` operator always returns a `float`, even when dividing two integers evenly (e.g. `10 / 2`).
questions.explanation_es: En Python 3, `/` es la división 'verdadera' (true division) y siempre produce un `float` (`10 / 2` da `5.0`). Para obtener un resultado entero truncado se usa el operador de división entera `//`.
questions.explanation_en: In Python 3, `/` is 'true division' and always produces a `float` (`10 / 2` gives `5.0`). To get a truncated integer result, use the floor division operator `//`.
questions.source: CPython docs 3.13 — Built-in Types: Numeric Types (int, float, complex)

questions.question_es: ¿Qué imprime `print(7 // 2)`?
questions.question_en: What does `print(7 // 2)` print?
questions.explanation_es: `//` es la división entera: divide y redondea hacia abajo (hacia menos infinito). `7 / 2 = 3.5`, y redondeando hacia abajo se obtiene `3`.
questions.explanation_en: `//` is floor division: it divides and rounds down (toward negative infinity). `7 / 2 = 3.5`, and rounding down gives `3`.
questions.source: CPython docs 3.13 — Built-in Types: Numeric Types (int, float, complex)

questions.question_es: ¿Qué imprime `print(-7 // 2)`?
questions.question_en: What does `print(-7 // 2)` print?
questions.explanation_es: La división entera en Python redondea siempre hacia menos infinito (piso), no hacia cero. `-7 / 2 = -3.5`, y redondeando hacia el piso (el entero menor o igual) se obtiene `-4`, no `-3`.
questions.explanation_en: Floor division in Python always rounds toward negative infinity, not toward zero. `-7 / 2 = -3.5`, and flooring it (the largest integer less than or equal to the value) gives `-4`, not `-3`.
questions.source: CPython docs 3.13 — Built-in Types: Numeric Types (int, float, complex)

questions.question_es: ¿Cuál es el resultado de evaluar `0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3` en Python?
questions.question_en: What is the result of evaluating `0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3` in Python?
questions.explanation_es: Los `float` se representan en binario de precisión finita (IEEE 754), por lo que `0.1 + 0.2` produce en realidad `0.30000000000000004`, que no es exactamente igual a `0.3`. Para comparar flotantes con tolerancia se usa `math.isclose()`.
questions.explanation_en: Floats are represented in finite-precision binary (IEEE 754), so `0.1 + 0.2` actually produces `0.30000000000000004`, which is not exactly equal to `0.3`. To compare floats with tolerance, use `math.isclose()`.
questions.source: CPython docs 3.13 — Tutorial Appendix: Floating-Point Arithmetic: Issues and Limitations (IEEE 754)

questions.question_es: ¿Qué función incorporada convierte el string `'42'` en el entero `42`?
questions.question_en: Which built-in function converts the string `'42'` into the integer `42`?
questions.explanation_es: `int('42')` invoca al constructor de la clase `int`, que sabe interpretar strings que representan números enteros y devuelve `42`. Si el string no representa un entero válido (por ejemplo `'4.5'` o `'abc'`), lanza `ValueError`.
questions.explanation_en: `int('42')` calls the `int` class constructor, which knows how to parse strings representing whole numbers and returns `42`. If the string does not represent a valid integer (e.g. `'4.5'` or `'abc'`), it raises `ValueError`.
questions.source: CPython docs 3.13 — Built-in Functions: int()

questions.question_es: ¿Cuál de las siguientes expresiones crea un string en Python?
questions.question_en: Which of the following expressions creates a string in Python?
questions.explanation_es: El texto encerrado entre comillas simples o dobles es un `str`. Corchetes crean listas, paréntesis (con una expresión) no crean strings, y llaves crean diccionarios o sets; además `hello` sin comillas se interpretaría como un identificador, no como texto.
questions.explanation_en: Text enclosed in single or double quotes is a `str`. Square brackets create lists, parentheses (around an expression) don't create strings, and curly braces create dicts or sets; also, `hello` without quotes would be parsed as an identifier, not text.
questions.source: CPython docs 3.13 — Built-in Types: Text Sequence Type (str)

questions.question_es: Los strings en Python son mutables: se pueden cambiar caracteres individuales en el mismo objeto.
questions.question_en: Strings in Python are mutable: individual characters can be changed in place.
questions.explanation_es: Los strings son inmutables: `s[0] = 'X'` lanza `TypeError`. Para 'modificar' un string hay que crear uno nuevo, por ejemplo con slicing, concatenación o métodos como `.replace()`.
questions.explanation_en: Strings are immutable: `s[0] = 'X'` raises `TypeError`. To 'modify' a string you must create a new one, for example via slicing, concatenation, or methods like `.replace()`.
questions.source: CPython docs 3.13 — Built-in Types: Text Sequence Type (str)

questions.question_es:
¿Qué imprime el siguiente código?
```python
s = "Hello"
print(s[1:4])
```
questions.question_en:
What does the following code print?
```python
s = "Hello"
print(s[1:4])
```
questions.explanation_es: El slicing `s[1:4]` toma los caracteres desde el índice 1 (inclusive) hasta el índice 4 (exclusivo): índices 1, 2 y 3, que corresponden a 'e', 'l', 'l', formando `'ell'`.
questions.explanation_en: Slicing `s[1:4]` takes characters from index 1 (inclusive) up to index 4 (exclusive): indices 1, 2, and 3, corresponding to 'e', 'l', 'l', forming `'ell'`.
questions.source: CPython docs 3.13 — Built-in Types: Text Sequence Type (str)

questions.question_es: ¿Qué método de string elimina los espacios en blanco al principio y al final?
questions.question_en: Which string method removes leading and trailing whitespace?
questions.explanation_es: `str.strip()` elimina los espacios (y otros caracteres si se especifican) del inicio y del final del string. `trim()` es el nombre usado en otros lenguajes como JavaScript, no existe en Python.
questions.explanation_en: `str.strip()` removes whitespace (and other characters if specified) from the start and end of the string. `trim()` is the name used in other languages like JavaScript; it does not exist in Python.
questions.source: CPython docs 3.13 — Built-in Types: Text Sequence Type (str)

questions.question_es:
¿Qué imprime el siguiente código?
```python
print("Py" + "thon" * 2)
```
questions.question_en:
What does the following code print?
```python
print("Py" + "thon" * 2)
```
questions.explanation_es: El operador `*` tiene mayor precedencia que `+`, así que primero se evalúa `"thon" * 2`, dando `"thonthon"`. Luego `"Py" + "thonthon"` concatena y produce `"Pythonthon"`.
questions.explanation_en: The `*` operator has higher precedence than `+`, so `"thon" * 2` is evaluated first, giving `"thonthon"`. Then `"Py" + "thonthon"` concatenates to produce `"Pythonthon"`.
questions.source: CPython docs 3.13 — Built-in Types: Text Sequence Type (str)

questions.question_es: Completa el f-string para que imprima `3.14` a partir de `pi = 3.14159265`: `f'{pi:___}'`
questions.question_en: Complete the f-string so it prints `3.14` from `pi = 3.14159265`: `f'{pi:___}'`
questions.explanation_es: El especificador de formato `.2f` indica un número de punto fijo (`f`) con 2 dígitos decimales, redondeando el valor. `f'{pi:.2f}'` con `pi = 3.14159265` produce `'3.14'`.
questions.explanation_en: The format spec `.2f` indicates fixed-point notation (`f`) with 2 decimal digits, rounding the value. `f'{pi:.2f}'` with `pi = 3.14159265` produces `'3.14'`.
questions.source: PEP 498 — Literal String Interpolation; CPython docs 3.13 — Format Specification Mini-Language — https://peps.python.org/pep-0498/

questions.question_es: ¿Cuál es el valor booleano del string vacío `""`?
questions.question_en: What is the boolean value of the empty string `""`?
questions.explanation_es: `bool("")` es `False`. En Python, las secuencias y colecciones vacías (`""`, `[]`, `{}`, `()`, `set()`) se consideran 'falsy'; cualquier string no vacío es 'truthy'.
questions.explanation_en: `bool("")` is `False`. In Python, empty sequences and collections (`""`, `[]`, `{}`, `()`, `set()`) are considered falsy; any non-empty string is truthy.
questions.source: CPython docs 3.13 — Built-in Types: Truth Value Testing / Boolean Values

questions.question_es: `None` y `False` son el mismo valor en Python.
questions.question_en: `None` and `False` are the same value in Python.
questions.explanation_es: Son objetos distintos: `None` representa la ausencia de valor (el tipo `NoneType`), mientras que `False` es un valor booleano concreto. `None == False` evalúa a `False`, aunque ambos sean 'falsy' en un contexto booleano.
questions.explanation_en: They are distinct objects: `None` represents the absence of a value (type `NoneType`), while `False` is a concrete boolean value. `None == False` evaluates to `False`, even though both are falsy in a boolean context.
questions.source: CPython docs 3.13 — Built-in Types: Truth Value Testing / Boolean Values

questions.question_es: ¿Qué imprime `print(bool([]))`?
questions.question_en: What does `print(bool([]))` print?
questions.explanation_es: Una lista vacía es 'falsy'; `bool([])` es `False`. Una lista con al menos un elemento, incluso `[0]` o `[False]`, sería 'truthy' porque lo que importa es si la lista está vacía, no el valor de sus elementos.
questions.explanation_en: An empty list is falsy; `bool([])` is `False`. A list with at least one element, even `[0]` or `[False]`, would be truthy because what matters is whether the list is empty, not the value of its elements.
questions.source: CPython docs 3.13 — Built-in Types: Truth Value Testing / Boolean Values

questions.question_es: ¿Qué operador se recomienda usar para comparar una variable con `None` (por ejemplo `if x __ None`)?
questions.question_en: Which operator is recommended for comparing a variable with `None` (e.g. `if x __ None`)?
questions.explanation_es: PEP 8 recomienda `is None` / `is not None` en lugar de `== None`, porque `None` es un singleton único: `is` compara identidad de objeto de forma rápida y no depende de un `__eq__` personalizado que otra clase pudiera sobrecargar.
questions.explanation_en: PEP 8 recommends `is None` / `is not None` instead of `== None`, because `None` is a unique singleton: `is` compares object identity directly and doesn't depend on a custom `__eq__` that some other class might override.
questions.source: PEP 8 — Programming Recommendations (comparisons to None use 'is'/'is not') — https://peps.python.org/pep-0008/

questions.question_es: ¿Qué imprime `print(1 == True)`?
questions.question_en: What does `print(1 == True)` print?
questions.explanation_es: En Python, `bool` es una subclase de `int`: `True` equivale numéricamente a `1` y `False` a `0`. Por eso `1 == True` da `True`, e incluso `True + True` da `2`.
questions.explanation_en: In Python, `bool` is a subclass of `int`: `True` is numerically equivalent to `1` and `False` to `0`. That's why `1 == True` gives `True`, and even `True + True` gives `2`.
questions.source: PEP 285 — Adding a bool type (bool is a subclass of int) — https://peps.python.org/pep-0285/

questions.question_es: ¿Qué imprime `print(None == False)`?
questions.question_en: What does `print(None == False)` print?
questions.explanation_es: A diferencia de `bool`, `NoneType` no es una subclase de `int` ni se compara por igualdad con `False`. `None` solo es igual a sí mismo, por lo que `None == False` da `False`, aunque ambos actúen como 'falsy' en un `if`.
questions.explanation_en: Unlike `bool`, `NoneType` is not a subclass of `int` and is not equal to `False`. `None` is only equal to itself, so `None == False` gives `False`, even though both act as falsy inside an `if`.
questions.source: CPython docs 3.13 — Built-in Types: Truth Value Testing / Boolean Values

questions.question_es: ¿Qué ocurre al ejecutar `int("3.5")`?
questions.question_en: What happens when you run `int("3.5")`?
questions.explanation_es: `int()` no puede interpretar directamente un string con punto decimal; lanza `ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: '3.5'`. Para lograrlo hay que convertir primero a `float` y luego a `int`: `int(float("3.5"))`.
questions.explanation_en: `int()` cannot directly parse a string containing a decimal point; it raises `ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: '3.5'`. To achieve this you must convert to `float` first and then to `int`: `int(float("3.5"))`.
questions.source: CPython docs 3.13 — Built-in Functions (int, float, str, bool)

questions.question_es: ¿Qué imprime `print(float("10"))`?
questions.question_en: What does `print(float("10"))` print?
questions.explanation_es: `float("10")` interpreta el string como un número y devuelve el `float` `10.0`. Al imprimirlo se muestra `10.0`, con el punto decimal explícito.
questions.explanation_en: `float("10")` parses the string as a number and returns the `float` `10.0`. When printed, it displays as `10.0`, with the explicit decimal point.
questions.source: CPython docs 3.13 — Built-in Functions (int, float, str, bool)

questions.question_es: ¿Qué imprime `print(int(3.99))`?
questions.question_en: What does `print(int(3.99))` print?
questions.explanation_es: `int()` sobre un `float` trunca hacia cero, no redondea. `int(3.99)` descarta la parte decimal y devuelve `3`. Para redondear correctamente se debe usar `round(3.99)`, que daría `4`.
questions.explanation_en: `int()` on a `float` truncates toward zero, it does not round. `int(3.99)` discards the decimal part and returns `3`. To round properly, use `round(3.99)`, which would give `4`.
questions.source: CPython docs 3.13 — Built-in Functions (int, float, str, bool)

questions.question_es: ¿Cuál de las siguientes opciones convierte correctamente el entero `42` en un string?
questions.question_en: Which of the following correctly converts the integer `42` to a string?
questions.explanation_es: `str()` es la función/constructor incorporado que convierte cualquier objeto en su representación de string. `string()`, `42.str()` y `toString(42)` no son sintaxis válida de Python.
questions.explanation_en: `str()` is the built-in function/constructor that converts any object into its string representation. `string()`, `42.str()`, and `toString(42)` are not valid Python syntax.
questions.source: CPython docs 3.13 — Built-in Functions (int, float, str, bool)

questions.question_es: ¿Qué imprime `print(bool("False"))`?
questions.question_en: What does `print(bool("False"))` print?
questions.explanation_es: `bool()` sobre un string solo depende de si el string está vacío o no; el contenido no importa. `"False"` es un string no vacío (tiene 5 caracteres), por lo que es 'truthy' y `bool("False")` da `True`.
questions.explanation_en: `bool()` on a string only depends on whether the string is empty or not; its content doesn't matter. `"False"` is a non-empty string (5 characters), so it is truthy and `bool("False")` gives `True`.
questions.source: CPython docs 3.13 — Built-in Functions (int, float, str, bool)

questions.question_es:
¿Qué imprime el siguiente código?
```python
print(''.join(['a', 'b', 'c']))
```
questions.question_en:
What does the following code print?
```python
print(''.join(['a', 'b', 'c']))
```
questions.explanation_es: `str.join(iterable)` concatena los elementos del iterable usando el string sobre el que se llama como separador. Aquí el separador es una cadena vacía `''`, así que los elementos `'a'`, `'b'`, `'c'` se unen sin espacios, dando `'abc'`.
questions.explanation_en: `str.join(iterable)` concatenates the elements of the iterable using the string it's called on as the separator. Here the separator is an empty string `''`, so the elements `'a'`, `'b'`, `'c'` are joined with no spaces, giving `'abc'`.
questions.source: CPython docs 3.13 — Built-in Types: str.join()
